Thailand. From September 15, visa-free stay is 30 days again, not 60

The special 60-day regime that was granted to citizens of about 93 countries since July 2024 is being cancelled. The new rules will start from September 15, 2026. Until this date, 60 days are still given at the border.

What's changing:
• Most countries, including Russia, USA, EU, UK, Australia - visa-free stay of 30 days.
• Seychelles and Mauritius - 15 days.
• Visa on Arrival is being limited; countries like Azerbaijan, Belarus, Serbia remain on the list.
• Those already in the country on a 60-day stamp can complete their stay. There is no retroactive effect.
• DTV, LTR, Privilege, work, pension - remain unchanged.

Why: in May, the government decided to close the gap for visa-runners, nominal tourists, and those living in the country for months. The usual package vacation (~9 days) is almost unaffected.
For Russians, the visa-free stay is not being canceled - they are simply returning to the old 30-day limit under a bilateral agreement.

🌐 Bitcoin price pulled back after briefly breaking above $82,000 on Sept. 4, as traders took profits following a short squeeze driven by softer Federal Reserve expectations and renewed demand for US spot Bitcoin ETFs. According to data from cryptonews, Bitcoin price traded near $81,150 at the time of writing, having failed to hold an intraday move above the $82,000 psychological level. The pullback left the asset about 1% below its local high but still well above the $80,000 mark reclaimed during the previous session. 

⚠️ The rally accelerated after Bitcoin moved out of a range around $77,000–$79,000. Short sellers were forced to close leveraged positions as the price crossed $80,000, adding automatic buy orders to the market. CoinGlass data cited by market reports showed that the broader crypto market recorded more than $500 million in liquidations during the rally, with short positions accounting for most of the total. Bitcoin shorts reportedly absorbed about $415 million of those losses.

📊 Price action has since slowed near a technically important area. Galaxy Research data shared by analyst Quinten François placed Bitcoin’s 50-week moving average near $81,041, almost level with the current market price. According to François, Bitcoin has not closed a weekly candle above that moving average since November 2025. He said a move through $82,800 would also produce the first higher high of the broader downtrend and bring $90,000 back into consideration.

"Linear Algebra with Applications" is a free and comprehensive textbook that introduces the computational, theoretical, and applied aspects of linear algebra.

The book covers topics such as systems of linear equations, matrices, determinants, vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, inner product spaces, orthogonality, and many more. The explanations are accompanied by over 330 worked examples, exercises, and practical applications in geometry, electrical networks, dynamic systems, probability theory, and optimization.

A particularly interesting section discusses how Google's PageRank algorithm uses the dominant eigenvector to rank web pages. The links between websites are represented as a connectivity matrix, and the components of its dominant eigenvector provide an estimate of the relative importance of each page.

This is a very clear example of how an apparently abstract idea from linear algebra can underlie a real-world technology used on a massive scale.

The 2023 edition is available under a Creative Commons license. This is another excellent resource that is worth keeping as a reference.

The Case Against Sanctions Skips the Numbers

A recurring argument in German commentary holds that the European Union has now imposed 21 sanctions packages on Russia to no effect, at rising cost to European industry. The second half of that is accurate. The first half runs against the European Commission's own accounting.

Russian gas fell from 45 percent of EU imports before February 2022 to 12 percent in 2025, according to the Commission's REPowerEU figures. Russian oil dropped from 27 percent at the start of 2022 to 2 percent, with two member states still buying. 

The Council of the EU puts both slightly higher, at 13 percent for gas and below 3 percent for oil. On either set of numbers, Russia has lost most of the European energy market it spent two decades building.

Europe paid for that. German manufacturers lost pipeline gas priced under an arrangement that assumed a different Russia, energy costs rose, and energy-intensive firms absorbed the difference. That is the real content of the complaint.

It leaves out what the cheap gas was. A price set below the market is a subsidy, and this one came from a state supplier that could withdraw it. In 2022 the supplier did.

The picture is also less settled than either side of the argument allows. EU imports of Russian liquefied natural gas rose in the first half of 2026 rather than falling. Close to 10 million tons arrived from the Yamal terminal alone, most of it landing in France, Belgium and Spain. 

The cargoes are legal: existing Yamal contracts are exempt until the end of this year from the phase-out regulation the EU adopted in January. 

What pulled them back was price, and the price rose because of the war with Iran. Europe's energy sanctions hold against Russian pressure and give way to a Gulf supply shock.

Russia has adapted, selling more crude to Asia and building networks to move it. Sanctions have not stopped the war. They have set a price on continuing it. Russian oil and gas revenues are down by more than a quarter. 

The government raised value-added tax from 20 to 22 percent and cut the turnover threshold at which small businesses have to pay it. The International Monetary Fund projects Russian growth of about 1 percent this year.

Reopening the pipelines would lower German energy costs. It would also return to Moscow the ability to raise them.

🌐 Coldcard hacker uses THORChain to swap stolen BTC 

📣 A hacker associated with the third wave of Coldcard wallet thefts began converting stolen Bitcoin into Ether through THORChain on Sept. 3, according to Galaxy Research’s Alex Thorn. The transactions moved approximately 10% of the Bitcoin controlled by that attacker. Roughly 90% remained at its original addresses when he published the update. 

🔖 Researchers traced the swaps through THORChain to a newly identified Ethereum address. Thorn said he shared the address with law enforcement, crypto companies and other organizations monitoring the stolen assets. However, not every transaction succeeded. Thorn said the hacker appeared to be experiencing technical problems while attempting to process the swaps.

🔔 The cause of the refunds was not immediately confirmed. Possible explanations include liquidity limitations, transaction settings or protocol safeguards, but no verified technical assessment had established the reason. The movement represented the first detected onchain transfer from the original addresses associated with the first three attack waves, according to Thorn. Analysts will now monitor whether the resulting ETH moves to centralized exchanges, bridges or privacy services.
